decisions.choice: Jonah son of Amittai: the prophet of 2 Kings 14:25
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 14:25 names "Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher", a town in Galilee, who foretold that Jeroboam II of Israel would win back the land from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah. Jeroboam reigned in the first half of the eighth century BC, about 793-753 BC, when Assyria was the great power to the north-east. The book tells a story about this prophet; it gives no date for itself.

decisions.choice: and the word came: the book opens like a story
decisions.reason: The book begins with the form that carries a Hebrew narrative forward, "and it happened" (as Joshua 1:1; Ruth 1:1). Most prophetic books open with a heading and collect the prophet's oracles; Jonah is a story about a prophet, and his message to Nineveh is only five Hebrew words (3:4).

decisions.choice: And the word of the LORD came ..., saying (L); The word of the LORD came to ... (B); The LORD gave this message to ... (R)
decisions.reason: The formula follows the wording set for "the word of the LORD came to me, saying", told here of another person. The colon leads into the LORD's words in verse 2, which take double quotation marks because the book is narrative and quotes speech as prose does.

decisions.choice: "Y vino la palabra del SEÑOR a ..., diciendo:" (L); "La palabra del SEÑOR vino a ...:" (B); "El SEÑOR le dio este mensaje a ...:" (R)
decisions.reason: The formula follows the Spanish of Jeremiah 1:4 and the term sheet for the prophets, with the opening "And" kept at Literal because the book opens like a story.

decisions.choice: "Jonás hijo de Amitay"; book-wide names "Nínive", "Tarsis", "Jope"
decisions.reason: The forms already published in Spanish (2 Kings 14:25; Matthew 12:40-41; 2 Chronicles 2:15). They are used through Jonah.

decisions.choice: "Et la parole du SEIGNEUR fut adressée à Jonas fils d'Amittaï, disant :" (L); "La parole du SEIGNEUR fut adressée à Jonas ..." (B); "Le SEIGNEUR a donné ce message à Jonas ..." (R); the prophet is "Jonas fils d'Amittaï", as 2 Kings 14:25
alternatives: "La parole de l'Éternel fut adressée à Jonas"
decisions.reason: The formula the term sheet sets for the prophets, from Jeremiah 1:4, so Jonah opens like the other books; the name as the published 2 Kings 14:25.

decisions.choice: Narrative in the passé simple at Literal and Balanced ("fut adressée", "se leva", "descendit") and in the passé composé at Readable ("a donné", "s'est levé"), with the imparfait for background; for the whole of Jonah's narrative (chapters 1, 3 and 4); the psalm of chapter 2 is speech
decisions.reason: French written narrative uses the passé simple; the Readable level follows the style guide and uses the tense of spoken French.

decisions.choice: "Giô-na con trai A-mi-tai" at every level
decisions.reason: The published form of 2 Kings 14:25, the same prophet, so a reader can connect the two; the opening formula follows the Isaiah and Jeremiah note ("Lời CHÚA đến với ...").

decisions.choice: "Neno la BWANA likamjia ..., kusema:" (L); "Neno la BWANA lilimjia ...:" (B); "BWANA alimpa ... ujumbe huu:" (R)
decisions.reason: The prophets' formula for the word of the LORD coming, as Jeremiah 1:4 and the term sheet for the Twelve. Jonah opens as a story, so the narrative -ka- form stands at Literal. Recorded once for Jonah, Micah and Nahum. BWANA is always the divine_name span with Yahwe as the alternative.

decisions.choice: "Yona mwana wa Amitai"
decisions.reason: The published form of 2 Kings 14:25, where the same prophet is named; "Yona" is also the form of Matthew 12:39-41.

decisions.choice: "{{divine_name:주|야훼}}의 말씀이 … 요나에게 임하여 말씀하셨다" (L); "…임했다" (B); "{{divine_name:주|야훼}}께서 … 요나에게 이 말씀을 주셨다" (R); "아밋대의 아들 요나"
decisions.reason: The formula "the word of the LORD came to me, saying" as the prophets' term sheet sets it [Jer 1:4], here in the third person; it ends in a period, not the English colon. "아밋대의 아들 요나" is the published form [2 Kings 14:25; Mt 12:40 요나]. Every YHWH in Jonah, Micah and Nahum is the divine_name span "{{divine_name:주|야훼}}" with the particle outside; "여호와" is not used.

decisions.choice: Narrative in the plain written style (했다) with -시- and 께서 for God at every level
decisions.reason: As the Korean style guide (section 4) and the term sheet: the narrator honours God with the subject honorific, and nobody else; God himself speaks 해라체 and never takes -시- in his own mouth.

en.L: "Arise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.B: "Get up, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, because their wickedness has come up before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.R: "Get up and go to the great city of Nineveh. Preach against it, because the evil things its people do have come to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} attention."

vi.R: "Con hãy đứng dậy, đi đến thành lớn Ni-ni-ve. Hãy rao giảng nghịch lại thành ấy, vì những việc ác dân thành ấy làm đã thấu đến tai {{deity_pronoun:ta|Ta}}."

ko.L: "일어나 저 큰 성읍 니느웨로 가서 그 성읍을 향하여 외쳐라. 그들의 악이 내 앞에 올라왔기 때문이다."
ko.B: "일어나 저 큰 성읍 니느웨로 가서, 그 성읍을 향해 외쳐라. 그들의 악함이 내 앞에까지 이르렀다."
ko.R: "일어나서 큰 성읍 니느웨로 가거라. 가서 그 성읍을 꾸짖어라. 그 성읍 사람들이 저지르는 악한 일이 내 귀에까지 들려왔다."

decisions.choice: Nineveh: a chief city of Assyria, later its capital
decisions.reason: Nineveh stood on the east bank of the Tigris, opposite modern Mosul in Iraq. It was one of the great cities of Assyria and became the empire's capital under Sennacherib, around 700 BC. Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and was feared for its cruelty in war (Nahum 3:1-4, 19). It fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.

decisions.choice: their evil: their wickedness, using a word that runs through the whole book
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word means evil done (wickedness) and also evil suffered (disaster, harm). It returns again and again: the disaster on the ship (1:7-8), the evil ways of Nineveh and the disaster God threatened (3:8, 10), Jonah's displeasure (4:1), the God who relents from disaster (4:2), and Jonah's misery (4:6). The repetition ties the story together.

decisions.choice: has come up before me: has reached me, so that I must act
decisions.reason: The wickedness is pictured as rising up to God, like the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 18:20-21). God has seen it and will deal with it. "Their" means the people of the city.

decisions.choice: the great city: "great" is one of the book's key words
decisions.reason: Nineveh is "the great city" (here, 3:2, 3; 4:11), and the story has a great wind and a great storm (1:4, 12), a great fear (1:10, 16), a great fish (2:1), great anger (4:1) and great joy (4:6). The command "arise, go" and "call out" also comes back: the ship's captain says "arise, call" (1:6), and the LORD repeats the command in 3:2.

decisions.choice: Arise (L); Get up (B, R); call out against it (L, B); Preach against it (R); come to my attention (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "arise", Balanced and Readable the everyday "get up". Balanced keeps "call out" so that the captain's "call out to your god" in verse 6 can be heard as the same command. Readable says what calling out against a city means, and turns the picture of evil rising before God into "come to my attention" (m3).

decisions.choice: "Levántate" (all levels); "clama contra ella" (L); "proclama contra ella" (B); "Predica contra ella" (R)
decisions.reason: Spanish "Levántate" serves for both "Arise" and "Get up", so one word keeps the echo when the captain repeats it in 1:6 and God in 3:2.

decisions.choice: "ha subido delante de mí" (L); "ha subido hasta mi presencia" (B); "ha llegado a mi conocimiento" (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of wickedness rising before God; Readable says plainly that God has taken notice.

decisions.choice: "Lève-toi" at every level, here and in the captain's words in 1:6
decisions.reason: French has one natural word for "arise" and "get up"; keeping it at every level lets the reader hear the captain unknowingly repeat God's command, as the English meaning decision at 1:6 notes.

decisions.choice: "leur méchanceté" (L, B), "le mal que font ses habitants" (R); the same root is "mal", "malheur" or "méchanceté" elsewhere in the book as the sense needs
decisions.reason: French cannot keep one word for the Hebrew key word through the whole book; the English meaning decisions point the reader to it.

decisions.choice: God addresses Jonah with no pronoun at L and B (imperatives alone) and with "con" at R
decisions.reason: The terms note: God says "ngươi" (L) / "con" (B, R) to a prophet; the Hebrew has only imperatives here, so L and B need no pronoun, and R adds "Con" to make the command natural. The relationship carries through chapter 4.

decisions.choice: "sự gian ác" (L, B); "những việc ác" (R)
decisions.reason: The meaning decision says this word runs through the book; Vietnamese cannot use one word for both the city's wickedness and the disaster it brings (1:7 "tai họa"), so "ác" is kept wherever the sense is wrongdoing.

decisions.choice: "Inuka" at every level
decisions.reason: Swahili "inuka" is both "arise" and "get up", so one word serves all three levels. It is kept the same in 1:6 and 3:2, where the captain and then God repeat the command.

decisions.choice: "ubaya" (L) for ra'ah throughout Jonah; "uovu" / "maafa" / "taabu" (B, R) as the sense asks
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses one word for Nineveh's wickedness, the disaster at sea, the judgment God relents of and Jonah's displeasure (1:7; 3:10; 4:1, 6). Literal keeps one Swahili word, "ubaya", so the thread can be followed; Balanced and Readable choose by sense, as the English does.

decisions.choice: No deity_pronoun span where the English has "{{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}"; God says plain "내" in 해라체
decisions.reason: Korean has no capital letters, so the deity_pronoun setting has nothing to change (Korean style guide section 7). Respect for God is carried by -시- and 께서 in narration and in human speech; God speaking of himself takes neither. This holds for Jonah, Micah and Nahum.

decisions.choice: "니느웨"; "큰 성읍" for "the great city"; "악" (L), "악함" (B), "악한 일" (R)
decisions.reason: The Protestant spelling of Nineveh. "성읍" is the published word for a walled city in the prophets; "큰" is kept at every level because "great" is one of the book's key words (meaning decision). R says the evil is what the people do, as the English R.
